cards.title: Read CAC Only Against Gross Profit, Not in Isolation
cards.summary: CAC is meaningless without context; judge it against gross profit per first order and over cohort life.
cards.use_when: Evaluating paid acquisition performance or deciding whether you can afford to scale spend in your store.
steps: Never judge a CAC number alone. Pair every CAC against gross profit (GP) on first purchase and GP over the cohort's life.
Compute first-purchase GP: take average order value at first purchase and multiply by your contractual gross margin (e.g. IM8's July figure: $212 AOV x 58% gross margin = $123 GP).
Divide that GP by CAC to get the 30-day (first-order) GP-to-CAC ratio. IM8 ran ~0.51 in July and ~0.4 in Q2 — low, meaning they rely on repeat purchases to recover.
Track the 6-month cohort GP-to-CAC trend over time, not just a single period. IM8's declined steadily from ~2x to ~1.03x across six quarters as volume scaled.
A rising CAC is acceptable only if AOV/GP rises proportionally and CAC does not increase proportionally. Increasing AOV while CAC triples can leave you worse off.
caveats: Low first-order GP-to-CAC is not automatically fatal — it depends on modeled repeat rate and payback tolerance you know you can sustain.
Cohort GP figures at 6 months may include only 1 month of data for the newest cohort, so treat them as directional, not final.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Question Any LTV:CAC Number: Horizon and Observed vs Modeled
cards.summary: When a brand touts an LTV/LTGP-to-CAC ratio, ask what time horizon it's measured on and how much is observed vs modeled.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your own or a partner's unit economics before scaling spend, raising, or benchmarking against competitors.
steps: When someone quotes an LTV or LTGP-to-CAC ratio (IM8 projects 3:1), ask two questions: what time horizon is it measured on, and how much of it is observed vs modeled?
Know the gap: IM8's 3:1 is a 36-month projection, but their oldest cohort is only ~20 months old — no cohort has actually reached 3 years.
Recognize that as you scale volume you usually push into colder audiences, which typically yields worse lifetime value per customer unless retention is actively optimized.
Note that changing offer structure (e.g. monthly-to-quarterly) and constant acquisition tweaks make historical cohort data less predictive of future cohorts.
Prefer a published cohort table (customers acquired per period and their GP growth over time) over a single headline ratio, because it lets you read the ratio at 6/12/full-cohort marks.
caveats: Repeat rates are fairly logarithmic and can be modeled reasonably for stable businesses — extrapolation is riskier when growth is very fast or the offer is changing.
A projection isn't proof of a lie; it's an inherent modeling risk you should price in.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Don't Be Fooled by Annualized ARR from One Strong Month
cards.summary: ARR is usually one month times twelve, so a single exceptional month distorts the picture.
cards.use_when: Assessing your store's revenue trajectory or a competitor/partner's reported recurring revenue.
steps: Recognize that reported ARR is almost always the current month's revenue annualized (x12), and growing businesses naturally pick their best recent month.
When you see an ARR claim, ask what month it was annualized from, or look for a rolling window instead.
For your own reporting, use a rolling multi-month window rather than a single month to judge trajectory and to set targets.
Apply the same skepticism to any partner or vendor claiming explosive ARR growth off one strong period.
caveats: This is a reporting-framing issue, not necessarily a falsehood; the underlying topline can still be genuinely growing.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Distinguish Cash-Flow-Positive from Genuinely Profitable
cards.summary: Financing that pre-pays acquisition cost can make a brand look cash-flow-positive while true profitability is unchanged.
cards.use_when: Interpreting 'cash flow positive' claims about your store or a partner's business when deciding to scale or invest.
steps: When you hear 'cash flow positive,' ask what is funding it. IM8's positive free cash flow came largely from a $1B facility that funds 70% of upfront marketing cost per cohort.
Understand the mechanism: the third party front-loads 70% of acquisition cost, so cash requirement on new cohorts drops ~70% even though the cost still has to be repaid later from cohort income.
Note that payback speed affects cost: if the cohort repays quickly the brand pays back less; if it repays slowly they pay back more.
Treat improved cash flow from upfront financing as a liquidity improvement, not a profitability improvement — actual profitability is unchanged.
caveats: This is not necessarily a bad structure — it substantially improves first-order cash flow — but it can be presented misleadingly as pure profit.
Do not assume you can replicate this; it requires large external capital.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Steer Awareness-Stage Traffic to the Matching Destination
cards.summary: Match ad-to-landing-page by stage of awareness: educate cold traffic, be congruent for problem/solution traffic, and send bottom-funnel to product pages.
cards.use_when: Deciding where each ad or campaign should link in your store's acquisition funnel.
steps: For high-awareness (unaware) or advertorial-style creative, don't push to a purchase. Send traffic to a third-party advertorial or quiz funnel whose objective is more education, on a separate domain.
For problem-aware and solution-aware traffic, drive to a persona-specific landing page with direct message congruency (e.g. match a GLP-1 ad to a GLP-1 page, a joint ad to a joint page).
For bottom-of-funnel retargeting (seen you many times, visited site before), drop them straight onto the core PDP so they can check out.
Sit your creative volume mostly at problem- and solution-aware stages; keep unaware ads a small portion (a big bet with lower hit rate) and don't over-weight product- and most-aware creative.
Match the claim sharpness to awareness stage: colder audiences need bigger pattern interrupts and more specific claims to cut through.
caveats: IM8 retired its quiz funnel in July, so funnel types that work can change — test rather than assume.
Aggressive cold-audience claims carry the most regulatory exposure.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Clone the Winning Ad Script and Swap Only the Persona
cards.summary: Use one proven script structure with a fixed mechanism and offer, changing only the persona to scale creative output fast.
cards.use_when: Producing ad creative at volume for your store when you have one or more proven winning angles.
steps: Pick your single best-performing script structure and keep the mechanism, offer, and format fixed.
Change only the persona or problem in each variant — e.g. a joint-pain version and a menopause version of the identical script, each driving to its matching persona landing page.
Recognize a 'new concept' doesn't require changing every variable; swapping just the persona qualifies.
Scale output linearly with spend: if you know each creative sustains a fixed average spend, doubling spend means doubling creative volume.
Bias toward video over static for mechanistic supplements, since video articulates unique mechanisms better and typically carries fewer compliance problems than image statics.
caveats: This only works once you have a genuinely winning base script.
Volume tracks spend, so plan creative throughput alongside budget increases, not after.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: The Clock/Timeline Ad Script Structure
cards.summary: A proven long-form ad format walks day-by-day transformation, naming a specific compound at each checkpoint and painting scenes instead of claiming outcomes.
cards.use_when: Writing or briefing long-form video ad scripts for a supplement or consumable product.
steps: Open with a symptom hook aimed at one specific persona or problem, never everyone.
Reframe the cause to something the viewer hasn't considered, then lead with the mechanism (the compound) before the benefit.
Walk a clock structure: 'on day 1 you'll experience X, day 9 Y, day 21 Z,' naming a specific ingredient, its dose, and its effect at each checkpoint.

Express every outcome as a scene and emotion rather than a claim — e.g. 'jump around and play with the grandkids' instead of 'improves arthritis.' This performs better and reduces (though doesn't eliminate) compliance risk.
Always close with proof, offer, guarantee, and scarcity. The clock doubles as a retention device, holding viewers by alluding to what comes next.
caveats: Painting scenes rather than making claims reduces but does not remove regulatory exposure, especially for aggressive cold-audience hooks.
This structure suits mechanism-heavy products (multivitamins, supplements) better than simple commodities.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Ladder Product Pricing to a Middle Option
cards.summary: Use a high price anchor (e.g. a premium bundle) to make the middle tier look reasonable and affordable.
cards.use_when: Structuring your store's product tiers, bundles, or subscription plan options.
steps: Offer at least three tiers: a cheap entry option, a slightly-below-middle option you want most people to buy, and a high anchor above them.
Let the highest tier exist largely to make the mid-tier look affordable (IM8's Beckham stack anchors the mid 'ultimate longevity' option).
Break prices down to per-serving wherever possible so the number feels more digestible.
Apply a visible ongoing subscription discount (IM8 uses a permanent 30%) with the subscription auto-selected by default, and show the higher one-time price as a contrast.
Be aware of the anchor mechanics you're creating: when a buyer strips the subscription/quarterly plan to get a lower commitment, the price jumps and the discounted plan looks like the obvious choice.
caveats: Representing a quarterly price as a monthly value may be non-compliant in some strict jurisdictions even if it converts; assess legal exposure against the gain.
Default-selected subscriptions can confuse buyers — IM8's own quarterly default surprised an experienced buyer at checkout.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Test Quarterly Plans for CAC Arbitrage, Don't Wholesale Switch
cards.summary: A quarterly subscription default can raise AOV, but only adopt it if CAC doesn't rise proportionally — test it separately.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to shift your store's default checkout from monthly to quarterly (or another longer commitment).
steps: Understand the theory: a higher AOV lets you pay more to acquire a customer — but only if CAC doesn't rise by the same or more.
Compute the arbitrage explicitly: if switching to quarterly doubles AOV but triples CAC, you're substantially worse off. The gain only exists when CPA stays below GP and you make more GP dollars.
Test quarterly-only funnels in isolation (separate from your main funnel) rather than switching your entire funnel, so you can measure CAC impact cleanly.
Lean in only if the test shows a real arbitrage (lower CPA than GP and more GP dollars per customer).
Note IM8 achieved a ~40% take rate on quarterly after introducing it, raising first-purchase AOV from ~$142 (2025 cohorts) to ~$212 (2026 cohorts).
caveats: The source strongly warns against switching your whole funnel to quarterly — it can wreck unit economics.
Case performance is an example, not a promise for your product or audience.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Offer-Stack the First Purchase (and Future Milestones)
cards.summary: Attach physical bonuses to the first order and additional freebies at future months to lift first-purchase value and retention.
cards.use_when: Designing PDPs, cart, and first-order offers for a consumable/CPG product.
steps: On the first order, stack tangible bonuses: bonus product units, storage, a mixer, a premium bottle — presented as a welcome kit.
Add a dropdown showing future freebies unlocked over time (e.g. bonus items at month 3 and month 6) to reinforce subscription retention.
Keep the visible tick-list short (IM8 caps it at a few core deliverables) because too many items dilute clarity; rotate which bonus you highlight and test what buyers actually care about.
Populate all bonus items into the cart so the value lands at the point of purchase.
In checkout, reiterate the guarantee (e.g. 90-day money back on quarterly), three core value props, and reviews — most brands under-use checkout.
caveats: Only applies where offer-stacking onto a first purchase makes sense; it won't fit every product type.
Use customer surveys to learn which bonuses actually drove the purchase rather than guessing.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Fix Social-Proof and Detail Discrepancies Before They Become Compliance Risk
cards.summary: Inconsistent claim numbers and ingredient counts across ads are a red flag, especially for regulated or public brands.
cards.use_when: Auditing your store's ad library and marketing copy for consistency and compliance.
steps: Scrape or review your active ads together and check that customer-count, ingredient-count, and proof numbers match across all assets launched at the same time.
Cross-check ad claims against your disclosed or actual customer numbers — IM8's ads cited 700,000 customers in places while finance disclosures showed ~414,000.
Remember the ad accounts of brands making outrageous claims get banned constantly, hurting CAC economics and making the business hard to sell.
Choose your lane deliberately: not aggressive enough and it won't convert; too aggressive and you risk bans and legal exposure. IM8 is seen as skirting the line near where they want to be.
caveats: Discrepancies may reflect product iteration or un-cleaned legacy ads rather than intent, but for a public/regulated brand they are still a compliance risk.
Some brands do run far more aggressive (native static) claims and out-earn compliant ones, but at the cost of constant account bans.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Persona-Specific Landing Pages Beat a Catch-All Homepage
cards.summary: Build a dedicated landing page for every winning persona/angle instead of routing diverse traffic to a homepage.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build persona landing pages and where to send varied acquisition traffic.
steps: For each new winning persona or angle in your ads, spin up a custom landing page and drive that traffic to it (IM8 runs ~150 of 700 ads to persona pages).
Write the page around that persona's specific problem — e.g. a GLP-1 page with '7 reasons GLP-1 users use IM8' and a bloating page with a gut-specific hook.
Maintain direct congruency: the ad message and the landing page message should match one-for-one.
Reduce homepage traffic where possible — a homepage carrying every persona at once tends to underconvert versus persona pages (IM8 still sends ~88 ads to the homepage).
Invest where competitors can't copy you easily (an ambassador wall, a proprietary science stack) rather than generic trust badges that everyone has.
caveats: Splitting into many landing pages is more work; IM8 treats it as an ongoing CRO testing roadmap.
Homepage conversion is skewed upward by organic traffic, so paid performance there is likely worse than it appears.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Make Your Value Props Actually Unique
cards.summary: Trust signals everyone can replicate (badges, generic reviews) carry little upside; profit lies in differently demonstrable proof.
cards.use_when: Differentiating your store's PDP or landing page trust and value proposition.
steps: Ask whether a trust element could be copied by any competitor — if yes, it likely adds little conversion upside.
Build at least one proof asset competitors can't easily replicate: an ambassador/celebrity wall, a proprietary science stack, or unique founder/expert credibility.
Layer trust: IM8 uses an ambassador wall plus a science stack as a second trust layer, both hard for competitors to match.
Treat genuine uniqueness as the source of arbitrage and higher paid ROI rather than piling on generic guarantees.
caveats: The ambassador-equity model is explicitly the least transferable part of IM8's playbook — you can't simply make a celebrity your co-founder.
Unique proof assets take time and money to build, so prioritize based on what your brand can realistically own.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Turn Escalating Costs into Decaying Margins via Equity Deals
cards.summary: Partnership costs structured as equity royalties fall as a percentage of revenue, opening margin as you scale.
cards.use_when: Structuring long-term partner, creator, or affiliate deals for your store.
steps: Prefer contracted equity/royalty deals over fixed fees where the partner is a durable growth driver, so the cost declines as a percentage of revenue over time.
Track partner cost as a named P&L line item so you can see it deleveraging — IM8's ambassador/royalty cost fell from ~14% to ~6.2% as revenue grew.
Recognize the model only pays off if revenue continues to compound; if growth stalls, fixed equity/royalty commitments stay expensive relative to shrinking revenue.
Weigh this against the source's warning that equity partner deals are hard to replicate unless you can attract top-tier partners.
caveats: This is explicitly flagged as the least transferable IM8 tactic for most operators.
Decaying percentage cost assumes continued growth; the deal structure doesn't protect you in a downturn.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Treat Operating Cost as a Percentage That Should Fall with Scale
cards.summary: Direct-to-consumer model economics come from operating costs shrinking as a share of revenue as you scale.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your store's P&L structure and forecasting when margin should open up.
steps: Track operating costs (people, R&D, overhead) as a percentage of revenue, not just absolute dollars.
Expect and plan for that percentage to decline as you scale — IM8 went from ~32% operating expense down toward ~15%, with a forecast near 11%.
Separate this from marketing spend, which you manage by MER: revenue spent on paid media (IM8 hit ~78% in Q2 2026 then fell to ~54% in July).

Watch the reported contribution margin definition: IM8 defines it as gross margin minus operating costs (advertising sits below it), which differs from the more common definition of gross margin minus advertising and marketing.
caveats: A 15% operating-expense ratio is still considered somewhat high; a projected 11% is a forecast, not a result.
When reading a partner's P&L, verify how they define contribution margin — non-standard definitions can flatter the picture.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Place Where Your Audience's Awareness Sits
cards.summary: The awareness-stage mix of your creative should skew toward problem and solution aware, not product/most aware.
cards.use_when: Planning your store's ad content mix across awareness stages.
steps: Sample your active ads and classify each by stage of awareness (unaware, problem, solution, product, most).
Aim for most volume at problem- and solution-aware, a small portion at unaware, and only a handful at product/most aware.
Treat unaware ads as a big bet: scalable if they hit, but with a lower hit rate, so don't over-prioritize them.
Let claim sharpness increase as the audience gets colder — colder segments need bigger pattern interrupts (IM8's unaware copy gets aggressive, e.g. kidney-failure-symptom hooks).
Accept that heavy up-funnel claims carry the most regulatory exposure and plan accordingly.
caveats: Numeric stage bands here are a read of a sample of IM8's ads, not a universal benchmark.
Colder-audience aggressive claims are the primary compliance risk area.
